newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Zaire jungle city returns to life with "liberation".
newsitem.headline: Zaire jungle city returns to life with "liberation".

text.p: The jungle city of Kisangani, made prosperous by diamonds and famous by books like Joseph Conrad's "Heart of Darkness", is coming to life after what residents call its liberation by rebels.
Hardly a building was touched when a motley crew of government troops and white mercenaries fled last weekend and the rebels walked in to take over.
The mainly Serbian mercenaries blazed a trail of terror in the month before Kisangani -- its years of neglect reflected in the weeds growing through half-finished buildings -- fell.

Formerly called Stanleyville, it is a commercial centre situated at the last navigable point on the great Zaire river but in the weeks that preceded the fall of the city, the mainstay diamond traders packed up and left, fearing violence.

Residents say people feared the Serb mercenaries led by a man they identified as Domenic Yugo, who witnesses say shot two pastors in cold blood last month while they held up their bibles and begged for mercy.
They equally feared Zairean President Mobutu Sese Seko's secret service, whose compound stands intact but empty after the liberation.

"These are the prison cells, and this is where they took you if they were going to torture you," a former inmate, Guy Rongorongo, 24, told reporters, pointing into a tiny room, little more than a metre (yard) square, with a rope hanging from its ceiling.
In the 1960's, Kisangani was the seat of another rebel government, headed by Christophe Gbenye, who fought the then Kinshasa regime of Moise Tshombe.

But the city is also famous for its portrayal in Conrad's novel, which a century ago painted a picture of a town blighted by darkness, savagery and irrational fear. And actress Katherine Hepburn stayed in the city during the making of the film "The African Queen".
More recently V.S. Naipaul's 1979 novel, "A Bend in the River", described the experience of an Asian trader washed up in the city in a post-independence country, spellbound by the "big man's" role.
The fall of Kisangani has broken the hold of president Mobutu, Zaire"s "big man", reviled by many of his own people.
Rebel leader Laurent Kabila, whose Alliance of Democratic Forces for the Liberation of Congo-Zaire (AFDL) hold a fifth of Zaire, is now referred to as the city's protector.
In a bid to capitalise on the expectations of the people, the AFDL has stabilised the exchange rate for the United States dollar and halved the price of beer, water and electricity in Kisangani.
It has also organised the election of local and regional leaders. The takeover has stablised some business and diamond traders are back.

But Kabila carefully resists the accolade. "I am not the liberator... I participated in the revolution. I don't want to be president. I want my people to be free and then I go back to my private life," he told journalists on Saturday.
